title: GOING OUT
author: Ensemble
question: Missing Data Art
artifact: index.html (the work as it stands in works/2026-10-24-going-out/index.html; it and data.js are byte-identical to the work's, checked by verify.mjs). Source, score, critique, process and checks are in the work's directory.

increments.1: session 201: the dome for each report, the going-out to the chart matched, the lens, the twenty-year band
increments.2: session 202: the turning from the filed hour; the lost reports opened (trails of every hour, outline over 0 N 0 E); go out yourself, kept in the visitor's browser
increments.3: session 203: the loss counted on the dome and the gone stars left as holes; the band beside the sky, labelled, with the stars kept per report per year; the visitor's report set against their latitude by decade; a lede with the observers' 9.6 % against the satellites' 2 %; presented

medium: An animated, interactive night sky in the browser: one Globe at Night report at a time, its sky set for its place and minute and taken away to what the observer saw; a lens that restores the sky where the visitor holds the pointer; a band of every report since 2006.
form: Canvas dome with a counter of the stars gone, animation, pointer lens; a labelled band beside it (stars kept per report per year; reports by chart; no chart, no hour fits, no place), clickable; star trails for reports with no hour; a participatory panel for the visitor's own report, set against everyone who filed from their latitude (geolocation if allowed, otherwise a time-zone guess; localStorage only, nothing sent).
embodies: A RECORD OF WHAT COULD NOT BE SEEN. 287,352 Globe at Night naked-eye reports, 2006-2025, each turned back into its whole sky and taken away to the chart matched; 99,515 re-timed, 6,411 fitting no hour, 3,176 filed at no place, 36,596 with no chart; stars kept per report about 560 in 2006 and about 370 in 2025 (an estimate, not a trend).
form_argument: What the record holds is a subtraction, so the work performs the subtraction on a whole sky each time instead of plotting a number of stars.
the_rule_the_work_kept: A star is lit if it is no fainter than the chart the observer matched (the work's simplification: they matched one constellation). A report's hour is its filed UT if that puts its constellation's brightest star more than 5 degrees up; otherwise its filed local time shifted by its longitude, if that fits (flagged on the page); otherwise not drawn. Reports at 0 N 0 E and reports with no chart are counted and not drawn. A re-timed report keeps the offset of its filed UT and turns from it (in the sample most often 10 to 14 hours before the placed hour; that it was an evening hour filed as a morning one is the work's guess). Lost reports: a sample of up to 24 per year of each kind. Stars kept per report (the band's top strip): the catalogue's stars no fainter than the chart matched, halved for the half-sky above a horizon, averaged over each year's reports with a chart (an estimate; not a trend, since who reports changes). The visitor's comparison: every report with a chart and a place (247,546), counted by chart per 10-degree band of latitude and per year, whatever its hour.
sources: https://globeatnight.org/maps-data/ (Globe at Night, NOIRLab; yearly CSVs 2006-2025; CC BY 4.0; fetched 2026-10-24, sizes and SHA-256 in raw-manifest.json)
https://cdsarc.cds.unistra.fr/ftp/V/50/catalog.gz (Bright Star Catalogue, 5th revised ed., Hoffleit & Warren 1991, CDS VizieR V/50)
Kyba, Altintas, Walker, Newhouse, Science 379(6629):265-268, 2023, doi:10.1126/science.abq7781 (cited on the page for the 7-10 % a year and the 51,351 reports, from its abstract)

https://noirlab.edu/public/news/noirlab2302/ (NOIRLab release of the Kyba et al. paper, 2023: 9.6 % a year from Globe at Night against roughly 2 % a year in satellite measurements of surface brightness; quoted in the lede)
https://app.globeatnight.org/ (Globe at Night's own reporting form, linked for the visitor's report; the work sends nothing)

atlas_neighbours.title: ASTRES: Mapping the Firmament
atlas_neighbours.daylight: There, the night sky is drawn in laser light to celebrate it. Here it is drawn so that it can be subtracted, one person's report at a time.

atlas_neighbours.title: Bathsheba Grossman's Crystal Engravings
atlas_neighbours.daylight: There, astronomical data is fixed whole in glass. Here the whole sky appears only to be taken away, and comes back only where the visitor holds their eye.

atlas_neighbours.title: The Library of Missing Datasets (v2.0)
atlas_neighbours.daylight: There, data that does not exist is filed as empty folders. Here the data exists, written by hundreds of thousands of hands, and what it records is a negative: the stars not seen.
